Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed retrospective real-world treatment cohort•September 24, 2026

Japanese lecanemab cohort quantifies screening and early ARIA

Of 321 patients screened at one Japanese memory clinic, 102 started lecanemab; among 70 with serial MRI surveillance, 8 (11.4%) developed ARIA within six months, while infusion reactions occurred in 28/102 (27.5%) and 13/102 (12.7%) discontinued treatment.

Key quantitative results: Treatment started in 102/321 (31.8%). Before amyloid testing, 154/320 (48.1%) were excluded or deferred after MRI/cognitive assessment; 54/165 (32.5%) who underwent amyloid PET were negative, and 13/102 (12.7%) treated patients discontinued within six months.

ManagementMRIDisease-modifying treatment eligibility

Added September 28, 2026 · DOI:10.1002/dad2.70492; PMID:42798750

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

This cohort exposes the operational funnel around lecanemab: only 31.8% of clinically suspected patients initiated treatment after cognition, MRI, amyloid confirmation and preference were considered. Early safety was broadly manageable under structured MRI surveillance, but four ARIA cases led to discontinuation and nearly one in eight treated patients stopped for clinical, logistical or financial reasons. The uncontrolled six-month cognitive data cannot establish effectiveness.

Study design

A Japanese memory clinic retrospectively followed 321 people with suspected MCI due to Alzheimer disease or mild Alzheimer dementia considered for lecanemab. MRI and structured cognitive testing preceded amyloid confirmation; 102 patients received at least one infusion. Safety and continuity analyses included all treated patients, ARIA incidence used the 70 who had serial MRI surveillance within six months, and paired cognitive analyses included 66 six-month completers.

Key quantitative results

  • Treatment started in 102/321 (31.8%). Before amyloid testing, 154/320 (48.1%) were excluded or deferred after MRI/cognitive assessment; 54/165 (32.5%) who underwent amyloid PET were negative, and 13/102 (12.7%) treated patients discontinued within six months.
  • ARIA occurred in 8/70 (11.4%) patients with serial MRI: isolated ARIA-H in 10.0% and combined ARIA-E+H in 1.4%, with no isolated ARIA-E. One macrohemorrhage and two moderate-to-severe ARIA-H cases led to discontinuation; a fourth mild ARIA-H case stopped because of advanced age.
  • Infusion reactions occurred in 28/102 (27.5%), most commonly fever (14.7%); 2/102 (2.0%) discontinued for persistent reactions. Among 66 six-month completers, MMSE fell from 25.0 to 23.9 (p=0.005) and CDR-SB rose from 1.56 to 1.77 (p=0.026), without an untreated comparator.

What changed

A newly indexed, source-date September 24 cohort provides a complete real-world screening funnel plus structured six-month ARIA, infusion-reaction, persistence and discontinuation data from routine Japanese practice.

Strength of evidence

Moderate implementation and safety evidence from a well-described real-world cohort with structured MRI surveillance. The single-center retrospective design, changing denominators, short follow-up, mild treated population and absence of a control group prevent causal efficacy comparisons or precise risk estimates for broader practice.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The study reinforces the need to plan MRI capacity, infusion-reaction management and counseling about treatment burden before initiation. Its ARIA estimates should not replace label-based monitoring or individualized risk assessment, and the six-month cognitive changes should not be interpreted as proof of benefit or failure.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to disease-modifying treatment eligibility, operational access, ARIA surveillance, APOE discussions, infusion management and persistence in routine care.

Access or reimbursement relevance

Lecanemab was covered by Japanese national insurance, but copayments of 10%–30%, frequent infusions and travel affected uptake or persistence. The study documents access friction; it does not establish a new coverage or reimbursement policy.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
How many screened patients actually started lecanemab?
102 of 321 (31.8%). Cognitive stage, MRI safety findings, amyloid negativity, patient preference and logistical or financial concerns all narrowed the funnel.
Was the ARIA rate 11.4% of all 102 treated patients?
No. The numerator was eight and the denominator was 70 patients with serial MRI surveillance within six months. The publication used changing denominators as patients reached follow-up milestones.
Did stable six-month cognition demonstrate effectiveness?
No. Only 66 completers had paired measures, MMSE and CDR-SB worsened modestly, and there was no untreated comparator.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective single-center cohort with modest treated sample
  • ARIA estimate based on 70 serially monitored patients rather than all 102 treated patients
  • Only six months of follow-up and predominantly CDR 0.5 disease
  • No untreated or matched comparator for cognitive outcomes
  • Selection, treatment-preference and attrition effects limit generalizability
  • Japanese eligibility, reimbursement and MRI practice may differ from other jurisdictions
